'''Max Black''' (February 24, 1909 – August 27, 1988) was a Russian-born British-American philosopher who was a leading figure in [[analytic philosophy]] in the years after [[World War II]]. He made contributions to the [[philosophy of language]], the [[philosophy of mathematics]] and [[philosophy of science|science]], and the [[philosophy of art]], also publishing studies of the work of philosophers such as [[Gottlob Frege|Frege]]. His translation (with [[Peter Geach]]) of Frege's published philosophical writing is a classic text.

==Early life and education==
Black was born '''Max Tcherny''' on February 24, 1909, in [[Baku]], then within the [[Russian Empire]] and now the capital of [[Azerbaijan]], to a wealthy [[Jewish]] family. The family left Baku whilst he was very young, emigrating to England in 1912 after spending a short time in Paris, France. The family name was changed to Black (a direct translation of "Tcherny") in 1911 or 1912. A younger brother, [[Misha Black|Misha]], became an architect.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Schrader |first=David E. |author-link= |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/ocm58455514 |title=The dictionary of twentieth-century British philosophers |date=2005 |publisher=Thoemmes Continuum |isbn=978-1-84371-096-7 |editor-last=Brown |editor-first=Stuart C. |location=Bristol, England |pages=93–94 |chapter=BLACK, Max (1909-88) |oclc=ocm58455514 |editor-last2=Bredin |editor-first2=Hugh}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Paul |first=Reilly |last2=Bagshaw |first2=Kaye |title=Black, Sir Misha (1910–1977), architect and industrial designer |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/display/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-30821 |access-date=2025-03-25 |website=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |language=en |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/30821 |doi-broken-date=}}</ref>

He first attended a free school in [[north London]], but at age nine was awarded a scholarship to [[Dame Alice Owen's School]], where he remained until the age of eighteen.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite ODNB |last=Singer |first=Marcus G. |date=23 September 2004 |title=Black, Max (1909–1988), philosopher |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/display/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-65646 |access-date=2025-03-25 |language=en |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/65646}}</ref>

He studied mathematics at [[Queens' College, Cambridge|Queens' College]] at the [[University of Cambridge]], where he was drawn to [[analytic philosophy]]. [[Bertrand Russell]], [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]], [[G. E. Moore]], and [[Frank P. Ramsey]] were all at Cambridge at that time and were influential on much of Black's later thought.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Wilson-Quayle |first=James |date=February 2000 |title=Black, Max (1909-1988), philosopher. |url=https://www.anb.org/display/10.1093/anb/9780198606697.001.0001/anb-9780198606697-e-2001666 |url-access=subscription |access-date=February 8, 2026 |website=[[American National Biography]]}}</ref>

He graduated in 1930, and was awarded a fellowship for research at the [[University of Göttingen]] for a year.<ref>Stroll, Avrum; Beloff, Ruth (2006) [https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/historians-and-chronicles/historians-miscellaneous-biographies/max-black "Black, Max"] ''[[Encyclopaedia Judaica]]''. (2nd ed.),  Garver, Newton (2005) [https://www.encyclopedia.com/history/historians-and-chronicles/historians-miscellaneous-biographies/max-black#3446800215 "Black, Max (1909–1988)"] ''[[The Encyclopedia of Philosophy|Encyclopedia of Philosophy]]''.  via ''[[Encyclopedia.com]].'' retrieved 11 March 2025</ref>

==Career==
From 1931 to 1936, Black was mathematics master at the [[Royal Grammar School, Newcastle]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Singer |first=Marcus |title=Biographical dictionary of twentieth-century philosophers |date=1996 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-06043-1 |editor-last=Brown |editor-first=Stuart C. |series=Routledge reference |location=London; New York |pages=[[iarchive:biographicaldict0000unse b8m6/page/74/mode/2up|74–75]] |chapter=Black, Max |editor-last2=Collinson |editor-first2=Diané |editor-last3=Wilkinson |editor-first3=Robert |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/biographicaldict0000unse_b8m6/page/74/mode/2up}}</ref>

His first book was ''The Nature of Mathematics'' (1933), a critical exposition of ''[[Principia Mathematica]]'' and a critical analysis of the [[Formalism (philosophy of mathematics)|formalist]] and [[Intuitionism|intuitionist]] schools of mathematics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ambrose |first=Alice |author-link=Alice Ambrose |date=1934 |title=Review of The Nature of Mathematics: A Critical Survey |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3746426 |journal=Philosophy |volume=9 |issue=35 |pages=362–366 |jstor=3746426 |issn=0031-8191 |url-access=registration}}</ref>

Black lectured in mathematics at the [[Institute of Education]] in London from 1936 to 1940.<ref name=":0" /> During this time he also undertook graduate work at the [[University of London]], being awarded a [[Ph.D.]] in 1939 for his dissertation on theories of logical positivism.<ref name=":1">[[M. H. Abrams|M.H. Abrams]], [[Sydney Shoemaker|Sydney S. Shoemaker]], Benjamin M. Siegel, Milton E. Konvitz, [https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/handle/1813/19225/Black_Max_1988.pdf?sequence=2&isAllowed=y "Max Black"] Cornell University Memorial Statement (1998)</ref>

In 1940 he moved to the [[United States]] and joined the Philosophy Department at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]]. In 1946, he accepted a professorship in philosophy at [[Cornell University]]. In 1948, he became a [[naturalized citizen]] of the United States.<ref name=":1" />

Black became the Susan Linn Sage Professor of Philosophy and Humane Letters at Cornell in 1954, a position he held until his retirement in 1978.<ref name=":6" /> He served as President of the Eastern Division of the American Philosophical Association in 1958–1959 and as President of the [[International Institute of Philosophy]] 1981– 1984.<ref name=":5" />

He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1963.<ref name="AAAS">{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter B|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf|publisher=[[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] |access-date=July 26, 2011}}</ref>

Amongst the [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] dissertations he supervised was that of novelist [[William H. Gass]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Schiller |first=Britt-Marie |url= |title=The dictionary of modern American philosophers |date=2005 |publisher=Thoemmes Continuum |isbn=978-1-84371-037-0 |editor-last=Shook |editor-first=John R. |location=Bristol |pages=891 |chapter=GASS, William Howard (1924–) |oclc=ocm53388453 |editor-last2=Hull |editor-first2=Richard T.}}</ref>

==Death and family==
Black was the elder brother of the architect [[Misha Black]] and the public relations manager [[Sam Black (public relations)|Sam Black]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arthurs |first1=William |date=2010 |title=Centenary of Azerbaijan-born London designer Professor Sir Misha Black OBE RDI PPSIAD FRSA (1910-1977) |url=http://www.londonsocietyjournal.org.uk/460/black.php |url-status=dead |journal=[[London Society (organisation)#Journal|London Society Journal]] |volume=460 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140219085120/http://www.londonsocietyjournal.org.uk/460/black.php |archive-date=19 February 2014}}</ref>

In 1933 he married Michal (or Mabel) Landesberg (1911–1985) with whom he had a daughter and a son.<ref name=":3" />

Black died in [[Ithaca, New York]] age 79, from a heart attack that followed surgery for cancer.<ref name=":3" />

== Philosophical contributions ==
Black made notable contributions to the metaphysics of [[Identity (philosophy)|identity]]. In a 1952 paper,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Black |first=Max |date=1952 |title=The Identity of Indiscernibles |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2252291 |journal=Mind |volume=61 |issue=242 |pages=153–164 |issn=0026-4423 |jstor=2252291 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Black presents an objection to [[Identity of indiscernibles|Leibniz' law]] – the principle of the [[identity of indiscernibles]] that states that no two distinct things can exactly resemble each other. He does so, as Peter Forrest notes, by suggesting "there could be a universe containing nothing but two [[Similarity (philosophy)#Exact similarity and identity|exactly resembling]] spheres" and that in "such a completely symmetrical universe the two spheres would be indiscernible".<ref>{{Citation |last=Forrest |first=Peter |title=The Identity of Indiscernibles |date=2024 |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2024/entries/identity-indiscernible/#Arg |access-date=2025-03-25 |at=3. Arguments for and against the Principle |edition=Winter 2024 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}}</ref>

He is also known for his interaction theory of [[metaphor]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Arseneault |first=M. |chapter=Metaphor: Philosophical Theories |date=2006 |title=Encyclopedia of Language & Linguistics |pages=40–43 |chapter-url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/B0080448542011949 |access-date=2026-02-04 |publisher=Elsevier |language=en |doi=10.1016/b0-08-044854-2/01194-9 |isbn=978-0-08-044854-1 |quote=Interaction theories of metaphor have a prominent place among contemporary semantic theories of metaphor. Introduced by [[I. A. Richards]] (1936) and Max Black (1962), this kind of theory proposes that instead of simply re-naming or comparing objects, two concepts or systems of associated commonplaces are simultaneously ‘interactive.’|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>
